title: Generative AI and the Courts: Expanding Legal Access or Opening the Floodgates? — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports AI as assistance rather than wholesale substitution and emphasises enduring human judgment, explanation and strategic counsel. However, it does not address whether automation removes the junior work needed to develop that expertise, nor does it propose reconstructed apprenticeship through simulation, mentorship or independent practice.
qs: Whatever the legal question was that led to the loss is probably something that humans are also important in (though other tools might help humans with that part).
But it's also true at the completely opposite end of the market, where your strategic partnership with a client that has hard decisions to make is going to be your highest human value.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The excerpt only introduces a programme that tracks AI developments for lawyers and judges. It provides no substantive claim or evidence about AI expanding legal-aid capacity, preserving human relationships, or producing proven access-to-justice gains, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.
qs: On every episode, we try our best to keep up with the rapid pace of change in the land of AI and draw connections for lawyers who are practicing all day, judges who are overseeing their dockets and may not have time to keep pace with AI developments, and think about what those developments mean in the legal profession.

st.t: AI competition: Distribution and habits rival capability
st.an: The source accepts a competitive landscape not determined by raw model capability alone and materially extends it by highlighting engineering innovation, published methods and potential imitation as constraints on durable platform dominance. Its DeepResearch experience also supports the cluster’s narrower distinction between useful background research and validated legal reliability.
qs: But even though they've all opened their weights, DeepSeq.AI still did this innovation in engineering that creates, I think, a better platform for lots of other innovators to use.
I don't know why everyone else can't just copy that now—because they did publish a paper explaining what they did.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI requires service and institutional redesign rather than tool adoption alone, and extends the proposition to courts and dispute resolution. It adds a concrete access-to-justice rationale while stressing that redesigned systems must preserve human explanation, dignity and strategic counsel.
qs: Maybe the parties will be able to work things out themselves and they won't need courts, or won't need arbitrators or mediators—but when they do need those, I want our operating systems to catch up to these new tools for the buyers and sellers of legal services.

I'm going to butcher it by making it really succinct, but essentially: People are willing to accept bad outcomes in court if they feel they were treated with respect and dignity—if somebody looked them in the eye and explained why they lost and what was going to happen next and why.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led division of labour and extends it to a concrete access-to-justice use case: automating front-end work for lower-value civil claims while preserving lawyers’ human functions and modernising court operating systems. Its claims of broader remedy access remain mainly predictive and partly vendor-supported, rather than evidence of population-level outcomes.
qs: I mean, there might still be problems if significantly more cases get filed in courts—we can talk about that in a minute—but I do think that the barrier to entry (those startup costs that make it impossible for lawyers to file a case where nobody disputes that someone was harmed and someone was at fault, but the injury is "only" worth, say, $75,000 or $50,000 or $25,000) is coming down.
Bridget McCormack: I think it's really important to remind lawyers and judges how much of what they do as humans is critical to their work.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source accepts the core shift from information generation to delegated action, describing agents as independently executing tasks across websites. It also frames legal AI primarily as augmentation. However, its account is tentative and secondhand, and it does not substantively address error propagation, verification bottlenecks or governance beyond an unsupported security impression.
qs: We've talked before about agentism—the idea that you could give an AI a task and it could independently perform actions to achieve that task.
Operator is OpenAI's—I think—first attempt at real AI agentism, where you can ask it to perform tasks on the web and it will autonomously perform those tasks by interacting with different websites.

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source supports the proposition by presenting an open-source model as a potential counterweight to concentration and citing rapid downstream reuse as evidence of broader participation. It appropriately treats greater competition as a forecast rather than proof that infrastructure dependence or market concentration has been eliminated.
qs: I listened to a lot of the commentary about it—much of it was confusing, with lots of numbers and debate about what really happened—but to me, the biggest takeaway is that this really could democratize AI development.
Hugging Face (which is an online platform where people share AI research and models) reported that by Tuesday—just four days later—there were 600 new models built with DeepSeq.AI's technology.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source endorses evaluating court AI against unmet civil legal need: it argues that cost and procedure leave valid claims unresolved, expects automation to improve practical access to remedies, and urges courts and dispute-resolution institutions to adapt. It also aligns with the synthesis’s bounded approach by preserving crucial human procedural-fairness functions and treating frivolous-filing risks and technological benefits as concerns or expectations rather than established outcomes.
qs: Bridget McCormack: I do think the ability for more people with non-frivolous lawsuits to get relief for those wrongs is a good thing.
Bridget McCormack: I think it's really important to remind lawyers and judges how much of what they do as humans is critical to their work.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central access-to-justice proposition by arguing that more valid, currently unmet civil claims should be resolved and by identifying low-value personal-injury claims as an example. It also aligns with the synthesis’s evidentiary caution: the excerpts express tentative optimism and trust concerns but do not demonstrate improved access, adjudicative reliability or outcomes, nor do they resolve the assistance-versus-machine-adjudication divide.
qs: Bridget McCormack: I do think the ability for more people with non-frivolous lawsuits to get relief for those wrongs is a good thing.
The filing requirements and procedural requirements for a civil lawsuit—even one where you're only alleging, say, $50,000 in damages—are really burdensome for a person without a lawyer.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s practitioner-led, cautiously optimistic approach: it favors using AI to expand relief for valid unmet legal claims and reports iterative professional use, while preserving human responsibility for dignity, explanation and procedural fairness. Its claims remain largely experiential and prospective rather than outcome evidence.
qs: Bridget McCormack: I do think the ability for more people with non-frivolous lawsuits to get relief for those wrongs is a good thing.
Bridget McCormack: I think it's really important to remind lawyers and judges how much of what they do as humans is critical to their work.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI-enabled legal services retain distinctive human value in judgment, explanation, client context and relationships. It illustrates that proposition through listening to self-represented litigants and strategic partnership with clients, but does not materially develop the cluster’s broader claim that institutional absorption governs AI value.
qs: Bridget McCormack: That's the example I always go to, the people who can't afford lawyers and how important it is to translate complicated, stressful processes for them.
But it's also true at the completely opposite end of the market, where your strategic partnership with a client that has hard decisions to make is going to be your highest human value.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source supports sustained professional learning and public-interest engagement with AI. It encourages lawyers and judges to interpret rapid developments and conditionally welcomes government access as a route to better public service and dispute resolution, while presenting these benefits as aspirations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: On every episode, we try our best to keep up with the rapid pace of change in the land of AI and draw connections for lawyers who are practicing all day, judges who are overseeing their dockets and may not have time to keep pace with AI developments, and think about what those developments mean in the legal profession.
But in a lot of ways, if governments get access to these resources, they can really provide better service to the people they serve.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source endorses AI as a bounded thought partner for drafting and iteration while preserving human responsibility for consequential strategy, explanation and client relationships. It directly supports selective augmentation, though it offers little evidence on verification costs, uneven productivity or junior staffing effects.
qs: So having this back-and-forth with an AI—and I'm creating documents, saving versions, iterating with different messaging, seeing how it feels for me, figuring out the best way to do this—it's just been a great thought partner on something fundamental to what I do every day.

I'm not saying you can't have a thought partner in your AI—you probably can—but evaluating the real-life implications of a bunch of different possible strategies is something humans are going to do with other humans, right?

kp.k: AI could make economically excluded civil claims viable
kp.d: McCormack argues that litigation costs exclude otherwise valid lower-value civil claims, particularly personal injury cases with undisputed liability. She gives $25,000, $50,000 and $75,000 as illustrative damages amounts that can matter greatly to individuals but cannot support conventional litigation economics. Her claim that AI is lowering startup costs and could give these cases a route to resolution is an optimistic market prediction, not a quantified finding about access improvements.
qs: There just isn't a way for lawyers to take on those cases because the cost of litigation makes it impossible for the numbers to work out.
I think this technology is reducing the barrier to resolution in such a significant way that it's finally giving that category of cases a place to go.

kp.k: Unresolved valid claims undermine confidence in legal institutions
kp.d: McCormack frames increased access for non-frivolous claims as beneficial to communities and the rule of law, rather than treating litigation growth as intrinsically undesirable. Leonard adds that AI could help bridge the gap between statutory remedies and the practical ability of ordinary people to assert them; McCormack agrees.
qs: I think the more valid disputes we can resolve, the stronger our communities will be and the more confidence people will have in the rule of law.
Right now, the legislature might create remedies, but there's nobody to help the average person actually execute them.

kp.k: Personal experience illustrates litigation costs and procedural barriers
kp.d: Leonard recounts representing her parents pro bono in a successful $15,000 insurance dispute that no lawyer would otherwise take. Full discovery, hearings and unfamiliar county procedures made the case burdensome even for a trained lawyer. This is a personal illustration of unmet legal need and navigation difficulties, not population-level evidence.
qs: I actually represented my parents pro bono once in a case like this—for $15,000—which to them was an enormous sum of money.
It involved full-blown discovery, going to the courthouse, having hearings and so on, and we did prevail.
even as a lawyer it was an incredibly difficult process for me to figure out how to litigate in a county where I didn't normally litigate.

kp.k: Streamlined trials offer a precedent for reducing resolution costs
kp.d: McCormack describes South Carolina summary jury trials as a privately agreed, one-day procedure using courtrooms and jury pools, time limits, a high-low agreement and a lawyer acting as judge. She presents them as effective at resolving claims too expensive for ordinary litigation while preserving an opportunity to be heard. Her attempted Michigan implementation failed to gain traction, which she attributes to lawyers' distrust; the example provides a procedural counterpart to AI-enabled cost reduction.
qs: So it's basically a streamlined jury trial process. The people involved still get to have their day in court—they get to tell their story, say what happened to them—and the jury makes a decision.
I tried to implement that in Michigan, but it never took off. I felt like the lawyers on both sides thought something was fishy—they couldn't trust it.

kp.k: Outdated filing systems constrain feared automated litigation floods
kp.d: McCormack reports concerns from courts about chatbots generating and automatically filing thousands of frivolous lawsuits, but argues these fears are currently misplaced because court technology and publicly funded IT capacity obstruct automated filing. She distinguishes generating demand letters or complaints from successfully filing them, and urges attention to resolving valid underserved claims instead. This is her assessment of present barriers, not evidence that frivolous litigation cannot increase.
qs: I usually can make most courts feel better because their tech infrastructure is so outdated. Like, automatic filing from a chatbot is far off.
But then figuring out how to actually file it is almost impossible (with current court systems).
I mean, this issue probably shouldn't even be among the top 30 things we're worrying about right now.

kp.k: Litigation platforms target case preparation and economic assessment
kp.d: McCormack describes EvenUp as a plaintiff-side software platform gathering case information, supporting liability and financial-viability assessment, and preparing demand packages. She says it enables attorneys to file more cases and attributes to EvenUp the report that customer firms collectively claimed or settled more than $1.5 billion in damages; this is a vendor-reported aggregate, not an independently established causal effect or solely settled damages. She also describes LegalMation's litigation automation, noting its pre-generative-AI history and potentially broader applicability than defense work, and discloses knowing its team.
qs: EvenUp's platform is doing all of that, and then it's putting together demand packages.

In fact, EvenUp reports that law firms using their platform have collectively claimed or settled more than $1.5 billion in damages, which is significant considering they've only been using the generative AI component of their work for a short time.
LegalMation is one that's been around a bit—they were using technology for years, even before generative AI, to enhance efficiency in litigation.
(Full disclosure: I know the team at LegalMation, and they're very impressive.)

kp.k: Dispute-resolution infrastructure must catch up with AI-enabled parties
kp.d: McCormack argues that courts, arbitration and mediation need more effective operating systems as tools improve for legal-service buyers and providers. She allows that parties may resolve some disputes themselves. She also welcomes reported government-focused products from frontier AI companies, expressing hope that public services will benefit rather than innovation serving only those able to pay most.
qs: Maybe the parties will be able to work things out themselves and they won't need courts, or won't need arbitrators or mediators—but when they do need those, I want our operating systems to catch up to these new tools for the buyers and sellers of legal services.
I was a little worried that all the activity in the market would be aimed only at those who can pay the most for the shiny new tools.
if governments get access to these resources, they can really provide better service to the people they serve.

kp.k: Human dignity and strategic counseling remain central professional value
kp.d: McCormack argues that AI should free lawyers and judges to emphasize respectful communication, explanation and human judgment about consequential choices. She invokes procedural-fairness literature without identifying studies, saying people more readily accept adverse outcomes when treated with dignity. She extends this role from assisting unrepresented litigants to strategic partnerships with sophisticated clients. Leonard supports the point with an anecdote about self-represented divorce litigants appreciating being asked about their experiences.
qs: People are willing to accept bad outcomes in court if they feel they were treated with respect and dignity—if somebody looked them in the eye and explained why they lost and what was going to happen next and why.
But it's also true at the completely opposite end of the market, where your strategic partnership with a client that has hard decisions to make is going to be your highest human value.
evaluating the real-life implications of a bunch of different possible strategies is something humans are going to do with other humans, right?

kp.k: Familiar framing and AI thought partnership support change management
kp.d: McCormack uses a historical horseless, horse-shaped carriage story as an analogy for helping legal audiences trust unfamiliar technology. Her proposed reassuring frame emphasizes continued human importance. She also reports personally using chatbots to identify stakeholder priorities and fears, tailor messages and iteratively develop communication documents; this is an account of her own workflow rather than a measured productivity result.
qs: Emphasizing how important the human parts are is the horseless carriage shaped like a horse, I think.
What are the priorities of the different stakeholders? Where might they be most fearful or worried?
I'm creating documents, saving versions, iterating with different messaging, seeing how it feels for me, figuring out the best way to do this

kp.k: Medical AI provides an analogy for task-specialized augmentation
kp.d: McCormack reports an unspecified mammography study in which AI outperformed humans alone and humans using AI, comparing it with an unspecified JAMA study. Leonard recalls about a 30% higher breast-cancer detection rate. Neither supplies study design, sample size or detailed comparator information. They use the reported result as an analogy: better technical diagnosis could leave human doctors, and similarly lawyers, more capacity for emotional support and strategic counseling.
qs: Yeah, it was radiology mammography, where generative AI was far superior to humans alone and even humans using generative AI, right? (Which is similar to what we saw in that JAMA study.)
I recall it was about a 30% higher rate of detecting breast cancer in mammograms.
You then need a human doctor to help you navigate what is a really difficult situation and help you strategize and plan, in the same way lawyers do.

kp.k: AI-supported learning offers benefits but risks becoming a crutch
kp.d: Leonard describes using ChatGPT to generate chapter quizzes while studying change-management literature for a book. She perceives improved question quality compared with a year and a half earlier and believes short quizzes reinforce learning. She anticipates applications in professional and informal education, while an example of her child wanting to copy chatbot output leads her to stress parental involvement and the risk of substituting AI output for learning.
qs: at the end of every chapter, I'm now going into ChatGPT and asking it to create a quiz for me to reinforce my own learning.
Some of the quiz questions it generated were confusing or flat-out wrong. But not this time!
The challenge we've talked about before—and I don't think I fully understand the instructions that come home—is figuring out how to not have them use it as a crutch.
And I could see it in professional education too—really, at all levels of education.

kp.k: Infrastructure investment and open models suggest competing development pathways
kp.d: The speakers contrast Stargate, described as an OpenAI–SoftBank–Oracle venture aiming to invest up to $500 billion without government money, with the Chinese model identified in the transcript as DeepSeq R1. Leonard reports comparable benchmark performance to leading US models including GPT-4, reportedly lower development costs and an approximately 17% Nvidia share-price fall. McCormack reports Hugging Face counted 600 derivative models by Tuesday following a Thursday release, described as four days later. Both acknowledge uncertainty about costs and technical explanations; democratization, faster innovation and redistribution of gains toward startups and consumers are presented as possibilities, partly attributed to outside commentators.
qs: Stargate was a joint venture between OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle aiming to invest up to $500 billion in AI infrastructure.
This company released a model called DeepSeq R1, and on benchmark tests it seems to perform comparably to the leading US models, including OpenAI's GPT-4.
Hugging Face (which is an online platform where people share AI research and models) reported that by Tuesday—just four days later—there were 600 new models built with DeepSeq.AI's technology.
Now, there's a lot of debate about whether the DeepSeq.AI team actually did it for a lot less money, and there's a bit more nuance to it than we first heard.

kp.k: Deep research tools could reshape lawyers' research work
kp.d: McCormack reports using Google's DeepResearch for background primers but had not yet tried OpenAI's version. She attributes to Ethan Mollick the comparison of Google's tool to undergraduate research and OpenAI's to PhD-level research, with reported completion times of 5 to 30 minutes or longer. Leonard and McCormack anticipate significant effects on legal research and analysis and reduced friction in obtaining advanced research assistance. These are expectations based largely on others' reports, not demonstrated legal-performance findings.
qs: I think he said the Google product is like an undergrad doing your research paper, and the OpenAI DeepResearch product is like a PhD student doing your research paper.
It's not going to give you an immediate answer—it can take anywhere from 5 to 30 minutes, they say (maybe longer if it's a really hard question).
And, bringing it back to law (which we'll discuss more in a future episode), this is what people hire lawyers to do: deep research and analysis, right?
Yeah, I think it's going to be very impactful for lawyers.

kp.k: Browser agents preview action-taking automation with constrained autonomy
kp.d: Drawing mainly on the Hard Fork podcast rather than firsthand use, Leonard describes OpenAI Operator as performing web tasks through a browser, with limited initial applications, confirmation before significant actions and human takeover for sensitive information. She reports refusals for some higher-stakes tasks and an erroneous grocery-delivery location in a reported trial. McCormack says she hears investor and legal-tech entrepreneur interest in vertical agents; legal-market implications remain prospective.
qs: you can ask it to perform tasks on the web and it will autonomously perform those tasks by interacting with different websites.
It asks you to confirm before it does any significant action.
Then it would handle any sensitive information by stopping and asking you to take over.
I keep hearing that "vertical agents" are what investors are interested in and what legal tech entrepreneurs are focused on.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack predicts that AI will lower the cost of pursuing economically underserved civil claims, increase lawyers' filing capacity, and enable more meaningful access to remedies, while preserving important human roles.
pts.d: McCormack argues that generative AI is lowering the startup costs that previously made lower-value civil claims uneconomic, especially where liability is undisputed. She expects resolution of more valid disputes to strengthen communities and confidence in the rule of law. Leonard adds that this could connect statutory remedies to an actual market for enforcing them. McCormack describes EvenUp as automating plaintiff-side preparation, case assessment and demand packages, enabling attorneys to file significantly more cases; she describes LegalMation as automating litigation work with potentially broad applications. These are legal-tool providers in the discussion, not alternative legal service providers delivering the work themselves. McCormack discounts an imminent flood of automatically filed frivolous claims because court infrastructure remains a substantial obstacle. She frames AI largely as augmentation: faster technical and administrative work should let lawyers concentrate on respectful treatment, emotional support and strategic client relationships. She anticipates that deep-research tools will materially affect lawyers' research and analysis. She also speculates that some parties may resolve disputes without courts, arbitrators or mediators, while calling for dispute-resolution systems to catch up. Government access to AI could, she predicts, improve public services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speakers offer professional experience, personal examples, company-reported results, articles and analogies rather than a measured estimate of AI's effect on court access or filings.
pts.d: McCormack supports the unmet-market premise with repeated reports from practicing lawyers and her experience trying to introduce streamlined proceedings in Michigan. Her account of South Carolina summary jury trials, including her husband's observational academic work, illustrates the value of reducing procedural costs but is not evidence of an AI intervention. Leonard recounts successfully representing her parents pro bono in a $15,000 insurance dispute that other lawyers would not take. For current AI adoption, McCormack cites recent articles and EvenUp's report that users collectively claimed or settled more than $1.5 billion; the transcript does not isolate additional recoveries caused by AI or distinguish claimed amounts from settlements. She discloses knowing LegalMation's team. Her assessment of automated-filing barriers draws on experience with courts and their IT limitations. The human-role argument invokes procedural-fairness literature and Leonard's recollection of IAALS interviews with self-represented divorce litigants. An unnamed mammography study, with Leonard recalling approximately 30% higher cancer detection, is offered as a medical analogy, not a legal performance finding. The deep-research discussion relies on secondhand accounts, including Ethan Mollick's assessment; McCormack explicitly had not tried OpenAI's tool. Government-service predictions rest on product announcements. No quantified forecast of additional suits, frivolous filings or court workload is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The episode presents cost reduction and vendor applications as already emerging in 2025, but makes broader forecasts without firm dates and conditions them on legal knowledge, infrastructure and continued human involvement.
pts.d: McCormack describes barriers as coming down now and current companies as early solutions. The strongest access claim concerns non-frivolous, lower-dollar claims where fault is agreed; she distinguishes disputed-liability cases rather than claiming all litigation becomes straightforward. She acknowledges potential problems if filings increase significantly. General-purpose tools can already help draft demand letters or possibly complaints, but users must know what to ask or learn the process, and filing remains difficult. Automated mass filing is described as far off because of outdated, publicly funded court IT, without a calendar forecast. Human strategic judgment and interpersonal work remain central even where AI is a thought partner. OpenAI's deep-research capability is discussed prospectively for the speakers, with reported completion times of 5–30 minutes or longer for hard questions; the PhD-level characterization is relayed from others, not established by their own testing. Independent party resolution remains a possibility, and improved government service depends on governments obtaining access to the tools.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central beneficiaries are people with valid but economically unserviceable civil claims; effects also extend to plaintiff and defense lawyers, sophisticated clients, courts, dispute-resolution providers and governments.
pts.d: McCormack emphasizes individuals for whom $25,000–$75,000 claims are financially consequential but too expensive to litigate under existing practices; Leonard supplies a $15,000 insurance example and raises business torts and insurance disputes alongside personal injury. McCormack tentatively generalizes the problem to civil wrongs below an unspecified economic threshold, not a universal legal cutoff. Plaintiff lawyers gain tools for evaluating and preparing cases, while defense firms and corporations can gain litigation automation; McCormack qualifies her understanding that LegalMation's applications are not restricted to defense work. Self-represented people may obtain drafting and procedural assistance but still encounter filing barriers. Clients unable to afford lawyers benefit from accessible explanations and respectful treatment; at the opposite end of the market, sophisticated clients continue to value human strategic partnership. Research-intensive lawyers face changes to a core service. Courts and public IT teams may face increased demand and need modernization. Arbitrators and mediators could see some matters resolved directly by parties, while remaining necessary for others. Governments and the public may benefit if AI investment reaches public-service institutions rather than only wealthy purchasers.
